outline.chapter_title: Case Background, Facts, and Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the parties, the Cameo platform, and the facts giving rise to the dispute. It covers how Kimmel used fictitious names to request personalized videos from Santos, which were then aired on Jimmy Kimmel Live! as part of a mocking segment. The chapter also outlines the claims Santos brought, the District Court's Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal, and the standard of review on appeal.
subtopics: The parties: Santos, Kimmel, ABC, and The Walt Disney Company
The Cameo platform and Kimmel's use of fictitious names to request personalized videos
The 'Will Santos Say It?' segments on Jimmy Kimmel Live!
Santos's copyright registrations for the videos
Santos's claims: copyright infringement, breach of contract, breach of implied contract, and fraudulent inducement
The District Court's dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim
Standard of review: de novo review and materials the court may consider on a 12(b)(6) motion, including judicial notice of copyright registrations

outline.chapter_title: Copyright Infringement and the Fair Use Defense
outline.description: This chapter explains the fair use doctrine as an affirmative defense to copyright infringement and walks through the court's analysis of the four statutory factors under 17 U.S.C. § 107. It focuses in detail on the first factor—transformative use—and addresses Santos's arguments that Kimmel instigated the creation of the videos and acted in bad faith. The chapter then covers the remaining factors and explains why the court concluded that fair use was so clearly established that it supported dismissal at the pleading stage.
subtopics: Fair use as a flexible affirmative defense under the Copyright Act
The four fair use factors under 17 U.S.C. § 107
First factor: purpose and character of the use and the transformative use test
Santos's argument that Kimmel 'instigated' the creation of the videos and was their 'designer'
The objective standard for transformative use: the perspective of a reasonable observer vs. subjective intent
Santos's bad faith argument based on Kimmel's false representations and Harper & Row
The court's rejection of the bad faith argument and the lack of market usurpation
Second factor: nature of the copyrighted work and the publication timing of the videos
Fourth factor: market harm—usurpation of a market vs. criticism or parody under Campbell and Hachette
Fair use as a basis for dismissal at the pleading stage under TCA Television Corp.
Affirmance of the District Court's dismissal of the copyright claims

outline.chapter_title: State Law Claims: Contract, Implied Contract, and Fraudulent Inducement
outline.description: This chapter addresses Santos's three state law claims and explains why each failed to state a claim. It covers the Copyright Act preemption question that the court declined to resolve, the direct breach of contract claim based on the Cameo Terms of Service and the third-party beneficiary doctrine under Illinois law, the breach of implied contract claim under New York law and the failure to plead essential terms or a meeting of the minds, and the fraudulent inducement claim's failure to allege out-of-pocket loss under New York law.
subtopics: Overview of Santos's three state law claims and the District Court's preemption ruling
The Copyright Act preemption question and why the court declined to resolve it
Direct breach of contract claim: Santos as a non-party to the Cameo Terms of Service
Illinois law on third-party beneficiaries and the presumption against conferring benefits to noncontracting parties
The significance of third-party beneficiary language in other provisions of the Terms of Service
Breach of implied contract under New York law: intent of the parties and surrounding circumstances
Failure to plead essential terms of the implied contract in nonconclusory language
Failure to allege a meeting of the minds that Kimmel would adhere to the Terms of Service
Fraudulent inducement claim under New York law and the out-of-pocket loss requirement
Santos's failure to allege actual out-of-pocket loss as required by Lama Holding Co. and Connaughton
Affirmance of the District Court's dismissal of all state law claims
